utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Madam Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. There are no preliminaries reported to the Chamber, which means that we could start hearing the evidence of the next witness. And the next witness to be called, Mr. Lukic, would be?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The next witness, Your Honours -- good morning, first of all, would be Mr. Trapara, Predrag.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then could the witness be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Trapara.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: From your answer, I take it you can understand me. Before you give evidence, the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration. The text is now handed out to you. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please be seated, Mr. Trapara. Mr. Trapara, you'll first be examined by Mr. Lukic. Mr. Lukic is counsel for Mr. Mladic and you'll find him to your right. Mr. Lukic, you may proceed -- yes, to your left, to my right. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Trapara.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Branko.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell us your name for the transcript, please.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: My name is Predrag Trapara.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you provide a statement for General Mladic's Defence?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at 1D1613 in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What's the ID number again, Mr. Lukic?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is this your signature on the first page, sir?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we look at the last page of the document, please, in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And is this your signature on the last page, please, sir?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now look at page 5, please. In both versions we need to look at paragraph 24.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember warning me that this paragraph is incorrect and that corrections need to be made?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm now going to read how the paragraph should go and then you can tell me if that version is correct. I'm going to be reading in English so that it can be recorded properly in the transcript and you can listen to the B/C/S interpretation. [In English] Paragraph 24, I quote: "The gas supply originated in Zvornik. The town of Sarajevo had gas. I know this because we had gas at the front lines which our soldiers used for heating. The water-supply to the town was not cut. It was not at all possible for Dobrinja 2 and 3 not to have any water because Dobrinja 1 and 4 which were under our control received water-supply through Dobrinja 2 and 3. The central reservoir supplying all the neighbourhoods in Sarajevo was located on Mojmilo hill, which was in Muslim hands." [Interpretation] Does what I have just read accord with how it really was?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The corrected version of the statement, does that now reflect accurately your testimony?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: If I were to put the same questions to you today, would you answer in the same way as is recorded in the statement?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes, I would.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I want to offer this statement 1D1613 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D1613 receives number D459, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D459 is admitted into evidence. You may proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. With your leave, I would read a short statement of this witness for the public.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Short?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Short.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It was longer yesterday, but after the warning you gave to my colleague Stojanovic, I shortened it down. Mr. Shin wants --

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yeah, I'm sorry. Just a very minor point. I'm sorry to interrupt, but I believe my colleague said it's a short statement, it's a summary, and perhaps that difference should be clearer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it is a short summary of the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Short summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed. I take it the witness has been explained the purpose of this so that the audience would know what your testimony is about. Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. [Interpretation] Predrag Trapara lived in Lukavica, a Sarajevo neighbourhood. He was the commander of the 5th Company of the 2nd Infantry Battalion of the 1st Sarajevo Mechanised Brigade, komandir. Quite some time before the war began in Bosnia and Herzegovina in September 1991, he saw Juka Prazina with members of his paramilitary group openly carrying weapons at Mojmilo Brdo hill. During the war his company was in contact with the 2nd Battalion of the 101st Mountain Brigade of the B&H army 1st Corps. At that time he knew that the opposing forces used 82-millimetre mortars as well as infantry weapons. These mortars were located in the civilian area of Sarajevo that was called Aneks. Throughout the war in the Sarajevo front, in the Sarajevo theatre, his unit carried out exclusively defensive actions. The line of separation between the warring parties was set in such a way that Serbs and Muslims came out in front of their own houses and dug themselves in. During the whole war, his company never carried out any offensives against Muslim positions for the purpose of capturing territory. During the entire war, the lines stayed exactly the way they were set at the beginning of the conflict. The bulk of the Muslim forces at that area was constituted by a large number of snipers. Serb positions and civilians were exposed to sniper fire practically every day. Predrag Trapara and his unit had information that the Muslim side misused civilian buildings for military purposes, namely, that they were firing from there at Serb positions or placed their staffs and commands there. The witness stated that his unit never opened fire in the depth of enemy territory but only at trenches and buildings where enemy soldiers were located. He's sure that at that time there were no civilians living in the buildings from which the B&H army was firing from. He never issued an order nor received an order to terrorise civilians in the city of Sarajevo or to inflict civilian casualties on the enemy. Quite the contrary, the superior command always sent orders to them that they should fire exclusively at enemy military targets. Mr. Trapara also stated that there were many civilian casualties on the Serbian side as a result of fire from B&H army members and that in the deployment area of his unit a lot of damage was inflicted on civilian facilities by that same fire. In February 1994, his mother was wounded in front of their house. She was wounded by rifle fire and both her bones below the knee were broken and to this day she has to use crutches. His father was also wounded by B&H army shelling as a result of which he lost his leg and his spleen was destroyed -- his liver was destroyed.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And soon he died because of the severity of his injuries. Members of his unit were locals, inhabitants of that neighbourhood. Convoys carrying humanitarian aid would pass through the territory where his unit was deployed and not a single one was ever prevented from passing through. There were instances of misuse of humanitarian aid by international forces. He recalls that on one occasion the military police discovered seven rifles in a humanitarian aid shipment intended for the Muslim part of town. Muslim units that were facing his unit frequently violated cease-fires. During each cease-fire, Muslim forces would intensify their works on digging trenches, and in that way they would be coming ever closer to Serb positions. Usually these works were carried out by Serbian civilians who were forced to do so. These were Serbian civilians who had remained in the Muslim part of the city. Having read the summary of the witness's statement, I would like to ask Mr. Trapara a few questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, perhaps for the next witness -- it was shorter. It still is not short. I mean, the 65 ter summary more or less would do. It's still two pages or even a little bit more on the transcript, too many details. So as you could keep that in mind for the next witness. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Mr. Trapara, were your troops surrounded by Muslim forces in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you one thing. Part of my unit was facing Sarajevo and behind our backs in the sector from Vojkovici, Krupac, behind Kasindol towards Kijevo, that means Karaula [phoen], Klanac, and Kijevo, that whole area was held by Muslim forces so there were two rings. We had one defence line ahead of us and another defence line behind our backs and that was the situation throughout Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now briefly about humanitarian aid, 1D2025, please, in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, is it correct that not all the headings in those documents are -- appear in the English translation? For example, if I look at the English, it starts what seems to be the seventh line in the B/C/S. The whole heading is missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Heading of what, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Of the original. Of course I can read that it's Republika Srpska and then the Presidency or cabinet of the president. And you see, I slowly get more familiar with even the Cyrillic B/C/S text. And then we have the date, the 7th of May, and we have a number and we have -- well, all kind of things which precede the text of the --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: You can in English here that -- now I can see that the translation is not complete.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Would you please take care that it will be completed and then uploaded again.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I do understand that the heading only says that it's the Republika Srpska cabinet of the president --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- strictly confidential, then a number, then Pale, a date, and then that it is addressed to the headquarters of the Army of Republika Srpska. Is that more or less what it says?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: That's exactly what it says.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, my staff is perfect in these kind of things. Mr. Shin.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We may have found another version of this. I'll leave it to my colleague to -- Mr. Lukic to decide if that's correct, but this may assist, that would be 65 ter 14545, but again I'll leave it to him to see whether this is indeed the document he is referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If that's the case, replacement of the translation would be easier. You may proceed for the time being on the basis of this document, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Thank you to my colleague Shin.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Trapara, here we have the document before us. Would you please look at it, specifically item 3 where the president, Radovan Karadzic, decided to enable undisturbed delivery of humanitarian aid to the areas held by the other side and says: "Effect the delivery of humanitarian aid as efficiently as possible with as little delay as possible and in a fair manner." You have spoken about this in your statement. I would only like to ask you: Was that the policy of both the civilian and the military authorities? What kind of orders did you receive in this connection, to let the convoys pass or not?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: We received orders to let the convoys through, and that we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would now like to tender this document to be MFI'd until we change the English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, the number would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D2025 receives number D460, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D460 is marked for identification. Mr. Lukic, would you also pay specific attention to the translation of the fourth item in this decision which ends by: " ... and concrete actions establish by negotiations." I could imagine that it should read: "Established by negotiations," so at least it's unclear at this moment what it exactly means. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I put a question to the witness in relation to this document? Sir, if you look at item 1 of the decision in front of you, I read there and I quote: "Stop immediately with all military offensive activities ..." How do I have to understand this? Which kind of military offensive activities is this referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Military offensive activities, maybe this pertains to another area of the theatre of war. The Main Staff is mentioned. Where I was on my defence line there was a kind of truce. Maybe this passage pertains to a broader area of our military zone. While there were any combat activities, I didn't know or receive a document of this kind. My unit never had a document of this kind. I believe this document was sent to units at higher levels, such as brigade and corps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: But to stop offensive activities means that there have been, in fact, offensive activities. When I read your statement, I form the impression that there were no offensive activities by the VRS with respect to Sarajevo. This strikes me. Can you comment on that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will try. I do not contest that there were offensive activities but in some other sector, in some other part of the BH. In the sector that I controlled with my unit, there were no offensive activities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps this is an order -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: No, please continue your sentence you have just started. Perhaps this is an order ... What kind of an order is it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps this was an order for the entire Main Staff, maybe in some area there were offensive activities at this moment and this order says they should be stopped, whereas at the confrontation line held by my unit there were none, at least if we look at this date here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I have one additional question as well. Do I understand from your answers that you have no knowledge of this order and the details of its content such as what kind of negotiations may have taken place? You see it for the first time, is that -- or have you seen it before, in what context?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have seen this order before, but I didn't see it at the time when it was written. And my unit was not at such a level that I would have been able to know what kind of negotiations were involved. I simply received orders from my own superior command, which was the battalion command, to let the convoys with humanitarian aid pass unhindered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You've told us that. Who has shown you this document for the first time, when you saw it for the first time? Who gave it to you to read?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I first saw this document in 2012.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And given to you by whom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it was the Defence team of Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please proceed, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I have a further question arising from your answer. You say you first saw this document in 2012. Do I have to understand that you had no knowledge of these orders during the war?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And you couldn't have acted according to this order because you didn't have this order?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In my statement it is written --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, I stop you there. Yes or no, you couldn't have acted according to this order because you didn't have this order during the war, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I acted upon the order to let the convoys through. I didn't know about this specific order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The orders that you received from your superior command, were they consistent with this decision of President Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: I believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now we would need 65 ter 15340.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We see the document from the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska dated 11 March 1995. It reports about the situation on the front, and now we need to see the second page in B/C/S and the second page in English. Let's focus on item 3. As you see, it says: "In the zone of the 1st Smbr, Sarajevo Mechanised Brigade, the enemy fired from infantry weapons and sniper rifles and 60- and 82-millimetre mortars. At about 1600 hours, the enemy fired snipers and killed two girls Natasa" and the name is probably Ucur "born in 1986 and Milica Lalovic born in 1984..." Is this last name correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At that time did you know about this incident?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes, I did. An hour after it happened I found out -- it's not the area of responsibility of my company but it's the area of responsibility of my battalion. So within one hour of the incident I found out by telephone that two girls were killed in Grbavica and we raised our level of combat-readiness immediately. So yes, I was aware of it very quickly after it happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What did you mean by raising your combat-readiness?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: That means reinforcing the front line and intensifying observation of the enemy because we were anticipating more enemy activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should like to tender this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 15340 receives number D461, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could we perhaps move to the last page with the signature. I see it's signed by Manojlo Milovanovic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Are you finished, Your Honour? Thank you. [Interpretation] I would now like to see P2050 briefly in e-court. [In English] It's document in English. I don't think there is translation so we can show it on the whole screen, and we need -- it's a code cable from Yasushi Akashi, UNPROFOR, from 14th of March 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, I see a translation into B/C/S. It's on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Is it there? I couldn't find. [Interpretation] We need item 3, in English it's on page 2, and in B/C/S it's straddling pages 1 and 2, I think. No, in B/C/S it's also on page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you this: At this time, on the 14th March 1995, were Muslim forces launching any offensives in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: At the time were there any Muslim forces on Mount Igman and on Mount Bjelasnica?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were there any Muslim forces in the demilitarised zone at the time?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes, that was the greatest problem. Yes. So in 1993 --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We're talking about 1995.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes. Between our lines and the Muslim forces there was UNPROFOR, and the Muslim forces used that time of this so-called cease-fire and they entered our territory unhindered by UNPROFOR in any way and they took tens of square kilometres of this demilitarised zone totally unhindered by UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were there any casualties on the Serb side?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: What do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Well, we know because part of my unit sent help to that area; that is to say, the area of Igman.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Because the Muslim forces passed through the demilitarised zone, were there any casualties on the Serb side?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you remember how heavy the losses were?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Well, I cannot say about the entire front line, the entire separation line. I can tell you about my battalion. Three soldiers were killed at the time, that is -- well, actually it was combat and it was not combat. The Muslim soldiers went through that area and they violated what we had observed, and that is how these unfortunate things happened to our people.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Did you notice any arming of the Muslim troops during the war?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Well, yes, I did. Every day during the war they were more and more armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I'd like to briefly show another document, 65 ter 08371. We need page 2 in B/C/S, page 3 in English. We need (c), 2(c), that's towards the end of the page in English and toward the end of the page in B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: This is what is stated here: "The Sarajevo-Romanija Corps," so it's the situation in that corps that is being dealt with. "In the northern part of the Sarajevo front, the enemy began with organised artillery and infantry operations on the area of the Nisici plateau in the early morning hours, focusing on the following directions: Breza-Cemera-Nisici and Olovo-Nisici ..." Do you have any personal knowledge about these attacks of the Muslim forces against the positions of the Army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So it's the 11th of April, 1994, that's the time-frame.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: At the time in 1994 in the area of Dernek, Korita, Veliki Jasen, Mali Jasen, Polom, Mosevacko Brdo, Stomorina, Vasevici, Nisici plateau, Hajde, Zubeta, Macak, and the village of Krivajevici, so along that entire line there were fierce attacks coming from Breza. Five of our soldiers were killed and then this was one of the stronger attacks coming from Breza. However, our forces repelled this attack and the lines were not broken. I know that throughout 1994 our battalion, including my unit -- well, we called that the Olovo front. All the way up to 1995 when those very well-known things happened in Treskavica.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: When you say very well-known things that happened in Treskavica, it's what we discussed previously; right?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes, because after that there were fierce attacks launched by the Muslim forces all the way up until Dayton was signed. Trnovo was on fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Were you personally at this part of the front line that is mentioned in this document that is in front of you on the screen?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I was there personally, and Obrad Popadic, chief of staff, a friend of mine, he was killed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to tender this document as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 08371 receives number D462, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I'm just going to put two more questions to you briefly. Did you know Radivoje Avram was -- actually, if you know the man, was his house in the area where your unit was deployed? Was Vojkovici under --

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: No, no, no, it wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Just tell us one more thing: Did you ever have an opportunity of seeing General Mladic during the war?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: I had two opportunities to see Mr. Mladic, General Mladic. The first time at Vrace when the Army of Republika Srpska was established in May and the second time was on the 12th of July, 1993, at Orlovac, the village of Ilovice, the first defence of Trnovo. The General passed by us, he proffered his hand. He said, "Congratulations, guys, and tomorrow I don't want to see any -- I don't want to see any other insignia on your caps except for the tri-colour." That is what remained in my memory in terms of the General.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: And what kind of insignia were on the caps in addition to the tri-colour?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Well, yes at that time -- well, you know, the army is the army so everybody likes some particular insignia. However, when the General passed by us at Orlovac, he personally said this to us and he addressed me. He said, "Tomorrow, I don't want to see any other insignia on caps except for our tri-colour."

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Trapara, that is all I had for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. Before I give an opportunity to cross-examine the witness - we might do that after the break, Mr. Shin - I would have one or two questions for the witness. Mr. Trapara, you told us that humanitarian aid was always allowed through and that even if it was abused. Were there ever circumstances under which you were ordered not to let through humanitarian aid, where it was prohibited for it to pass through?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I tell you, Your Honour, maybe sometimes there were some orders, but I said a moment ago I did not know. Believe me, I always allowed convoys to go in the direction of Grbavica at that. I personally as far as my superior command was concerned, my battalion command, never sent me an order like that to stop a convoy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Same question for movement of humanitarian organisations, were they ever prohibited to move around freely?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I know to the best of my knowledge at that time, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now, sometimes nasty events happened. You referred to the killing of two young girls which is really very nasty that this ever happened in the age of 8, 10 years, innocent children. Did such events not trigger a prohibition of humanitarian aid or a prohibition of movement of humanitarian organisations?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Specifically where we were, no. Most of that, after all, was -- I mean, well, the entire town went through Lukavica, I mean all of the humanitarian aid. On that day when the two little girls were killed, we did not receive an order to stop humanitarian aid convoys.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I have D461 on the screen, please, page 3 in English. I don't know whether it's also page 3 in B/C/S. Could I invite you to read the paragraph, especially the last sentence of the paragraph II, situation in the territory. I will read it aloud for you. "Due to sniper fire and the death of two girls, any movement of humanitarian organisations and convoys is prohibited until further notice." In view of your testimony, do I have to understand that this order which was so specifically focusing on the death of the two girls never reached you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Believe me, no. According to this document, it seems that I violated an order, but this order did not reach me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for those answers. Judge Fluegge has one more question for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I have a question also in relation to the convoys, and I would like to ask that D459 should be brought up on the screen, paragraph 22 in both languages. And I quote from your statement: "Convoys passed through daily and always allowed them to pass into the town. Convoys were searched exclusively by the corps police." And now please focus on the next sentence because I don't understand that. I quote: "Did they ever receive an order to fire on civilians or civilian facilities, he answers that they did not, nor did he ever issue such an order." How do I have to understand this sentence, especially the "he"? Who is "he"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, I just don't understand, which paragraph is this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It's paragraph 22 at the end, the last sentence, in fact. "Did they ever receive an order to fire on civilians or civilian facilities, he answers that they did not, nor did he ever issue such an order."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It probably relates to me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Then it's perhaps not properly drafted by the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I noticed that, Your Honour, this morning when I was re-reading the statement. Obviously we left in the third person this part of the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we first take the break and we'll start the cross-examination after the break. We'll resume at ten minutes to 11.00 and we'll take the break once the witness has been escorted out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We're waiting for the witness to be escorted into the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Trapara, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Shin. Mr. Shin is located to your right. Mr. Shin is counsel for the Prosecution. Mr. Shin, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Trapara.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: I'd like to begin with some questions about your unit. Now, you were, as you explain in your statement, in the 1st Sarajevo Mechanised Brigade, 2nd Battalion, 5th Company. This battalion, as you explain also, was originally the 3rd Battalion of the 1st Romanija Brigade and then it became the 2nd Battalion in the 1st Sarajevo Mechanised Brigade in May 1993. We have that correct; right?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, regardless of the name of your unit or the designation it had, your company's zone of responsibility did not change during the war; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, as company commander, you held the rank of captain; right?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And you were a captain throughout the war?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: When the war started, I was a lieutenant.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: When were you promoted?

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, as company commander, who was your immediate superior?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: I had three battalion commanders. They changed. I can tell you the order of their names, if you need me to.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: If you could briefly tell us their names.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: The first commander was Mr. Brane Plakalovic. Very shortly after him, he was wounded, so shortly after him it was Mr. Radomir Stojanovic. He was killed in 1993. And then after that it was Mr. Aleksandar Petrovic who died. From what I know he died in America.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, Aleksandar Petrovic, he became commander approximately when in 1993?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: In early 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Would it be right that the deputy commander for your battalion was Milan Hrvacevic?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes, but at a later stage of the conflict, not right at the beginning but later. Perhaps a year before the conflict ended.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: So that would be in 1994; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Approximately. Don't expect me to know the exact month, but approximately yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And the assistant commander for intelligence and security in your battalion was Dragan Maletic; correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes, also in the second half, in the second half.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, where was the 2nd Battalion's command post?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: The 2nd Battalion's command post was located in Banjalucka Street.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: What neighbourhood was that?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: It was between Grbavica and Vrace where the transit is, above the transit. I'm thinking about the roundabout.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Okay. We'll get to that later. Where was the command post for your company?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: My company's command post was in the Lukavica sector, Djukica Potok creek. It was a private house. That belonged to Rajko Tomic.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Okay. We may look at a map later where you can show us where that was. Now, the 2nd Battalion had six infantry companies; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: What other units were attached to this battalion or under it?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: There was a squad or a platoon of 82-millimetre mortars.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And we'll get to that shortly as well. Were there any other units in the battalion, apart from that?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: If you're thinking about signals, the logistics units, that's what else there would be more or less.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Okay. Now, as an infantry officer, as a captain, would it be correct that you also knew which units were part of the 1st Sarajevo Mechanised Brigade? In other words, above the level of the battalion?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Up to a point, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Well, let me ask you, for example, in addition to infantry battalions such as the one that you belonged to, the 1st Sarajevo Mechanised Brigade also had a mixed artillery division; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: It also had an armoured battalion; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Can you tell us what other components of the 1st Sarajevo Mechanised Brigade you can recall?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: It had a logistics battalion, a signals company, engineers company, another armoured battalion, military police, and what you mentioned, that would be that and also the brigade command.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Okay. Just so we're clear here, there were then two armoured battalions; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to focus on your company. Now, in your company you had some 100 to 180 men; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: The second number would refer to people who were in the company at some point but then went elsewhere. A lot of people came through the company, but the actual number would be approximately 130 men.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And these men were organised in four platoons?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: As company commander you issued orders to your platoon commanders; that's simply a fundamental principle of command and control. Correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And they followed your orders; that's how command and control operates?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And did -- if they had acted outside your orders or in violation of your orders, as their leader you would have had to take corrective action?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, regarding the levels of command above you, you've previously testified in the Dragomir Milosevic case that during your time -- during the time that you served with the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, the corps had a functioning chain of command, from the corps to the brigade to battalion levels. So again, the levels above your command, the chain of function -- the chain of command functioned; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: As company commander, now, you were responsible for the safety of your men, among other things; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: In the military a component of ensuring the safety of your men as a commander is having situational awareness; that is, knowing the situation in the field, in particular regarding your enemy and regarding your own forces?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: If there was information about the enemy.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: But otherwise, you accept what I said?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: I do, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Your men, in fact, rely on you as their commander to have this kind of situational awareness; that's part of maintaining their safety?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, let's turn to a map that you've seen before.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Can I please have 65 ter 1D02064 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. Trapara, you recognise this as a map that you have previously seen that was tendered as an associated exhibit to your Karadzic testimony -- I'm sorry, to your Karadzic statement. You recognise the map; correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: I do, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, it's in English but do you understand what it says?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, off to the right that red circle with the arrow pointing to it, that shows the location of three 82-millimetre mortars on Prljevo Brdo; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Which circle? Mr. Shin, is that the one in which "Aneks" is written or the other one to the further side?

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, it's the small circle to the right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes, but that's correct that those -- that's correct that there were three 82-millimetre mortars there, first?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes, it's correct. It's a three 82-millimetre battery that was under the direct command of our battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Just -- yes, you're pointing at the circle, the thick one, right to 2nd Battalion. Yes, I see it now because part is -- it says 3 and half of an M, but it's the lower thick circle.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Could I please have the court officer simply move the map a little bit over so that we can see clearly what Mr. President is reading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Now it's clear to me, yes. It's next to where it's written "Turbe" and 3MB, 82-millimetre.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And Mr. Trapara, just in case we lost that there, that location, you understand that to be Prljevo Brdo or Prljevo hill; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now we'll return to this, and you may get some other questions on this map, but I'd like to move --

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours, first may I tender this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D2064 receives number P6514, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: P6514 is admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. Trapara, I'd like to focus on the front line for now and for that I'll turn to a different map that you marked in your testimony in the Dragomir Milosevic case.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Could I please have 65 ter 30649.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Do you recognise this map to be a map that you marked during your testimony in the Dragomir Milosevic trial?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I recognise it, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to focus on the red line. That is the line of confrontation; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And just so we have a complete picture here, the blue line is what you intended to be your company's area of responsibility along that line of confrontation?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: The blue line indicates already the line of the B&H army forces that were across from us already. The blue circle was marking the depth of the territory of the 2nd Battalion of the 101st Mountain Brigade of the B&H army.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: To assist us, could you tell us what stretch of that red line was the area of responsibility of your company?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: The straight blue line, as you look at it, from the left end of the blue line until the end of the blue line and a little bit longer to the place where these two red lines merge.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Okay. I think that description can help us orient ourselves on that map.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, you indicated the line of confrontation with that red line because you know this area well; correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, would it be right that to the right side of this diagram past the end of the area of responsibility that your company held, there was the 4th Company of your battalion?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And on the other side of that company, which unit held the line?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: The 6th Company.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And on the other side of the 6th Company?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Then it was the 3rd Company all the way to the Zeljeznica club stadium.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, let's turn to the left side of this line. You described in your Milosevic testimony that it went through Dobrinja 4, and indeed we see it extending further south; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: What I showed here was the line of separation during the Dayton. While the conflict was still going on, the line was at Dobrinja 4, Dobrinja 1, and then the Staro Sedelaca [phoen] settlement where the red line curves. And then later the line was extended a bit longer towards the Serbian side.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Okay. Maybe if we could have a pen for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. Trapara, could you please indicate where the confrontation line was during the war in relation to the red line.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Are we talking about Dobrinja?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Shin, are you going to invite the witness to mark further with a red pen ?

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: We would prefer to have a new colour other than --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: A new colour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: -- yes. Sorry, I should have been clear about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, because if any additional marking is made, it should be clearly distinguished from the already existing blue and red marking. Do we have green for the witness? And then could you please repeat your instruction to the witness, Mr. Shin.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. Trapara, once again I'm asking you to indicate where the line of confrontation was during the war in the Dobrinja area.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: I already marked the red line here. During the war the line of confrontation was where I marked it, this red line. We're talking about Dobrinja 1 and Dobrinja 4.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Okay. I think we're clear now that that red line actually is the confrontation line during the war and not some other line; correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Correct. That was the confrontation line during the war, the red line.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, in your statement you say that the unit to your left was the engineering company of the 1st Sarajevo Brigade. Now, first, by the "1st Sarajevo Brigade," you do mean the same thing as the 1st Sarajevo Mechanised Brigade; correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Indeed, that's sometimes the way the 1st Sarajevo Mechanised Brigade was referred to, as the 1st Sarajevo Brigade?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: It was shorter so that's how most people named the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And this engineering company is the one you spoke of as being directly attached to the brigade; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Who was on the other side of the engineering company on the Serb lines?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: The 2nd Battalion of the 101st Mountain Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Perhaps my question was unclear. Among the VRS units, which unit was on the other side of the engineering company?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: I'm sorry, yes. In Dobrinja 4 and Dobrinja 1 there was a part of -- to the left of the engineering company there was a unit comprising soldiers from the 1st Armoured Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Trapara, you're familiar with this area not only because you were an infantry commander during the war but also because you lived in this area most of your life; is that right?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: I was born here, right here on this line that you are mentioning between the two Dobrinjas. I grew up there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, you're familiar with an area called Veljine just to the east of Dobrinja 4; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And there is an Orthodox church there, that's the Vasilije Ostroski church?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: I'd like to move to another document. Could I please have P4455. And while that's coming up, could I please tender into evidence this map which is 65 ter 30649.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: With or without the additional markings? I see there are two green, there's a 1 and what appears to be a 2 but close to the confrontation line, but the witness spoke about the Dobrinja 4 so I'm a bit confused. But I think we can do without the markings.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: I think we -- yes, absolutely, Mr. President, we can do without the markings because the witness had corrected himself to indicate --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: -- that that red line was what we were looking at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, the map as previously marked by the witness with red and blue would receive number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 30649 receives number P6515, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Could I please have P4455 now on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Witness, this is a report as you can see from the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps command dated 14th of June, 1992. If we look at the back briefly we see it's signed by Commander Colonel Tomislav Sipcic. And turning back to the front page, do you see the heading number 1, Sarajevska Brigada, that's in your language. Now, would that refer to the Sarajevo Mechanised Brigade?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Looking down at item number 9 under this first -- under the heading "Sarajevo Brigade," it reads: "1 self-propelled artillery battery from composition of 1st Sarajevo Brigade with one platoon on Veljine (the church), and with the 2nd Platoon in village Vranjes." Do you understand this document to mean that there was an artillery battery at the 1st Sarajevo Mechanised Brigade that held that position?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: It says here one squad from the 1st Sarajevo Brigade with one platoon on Veljine at the church and another platoon in the village of Vranjes. So one weak PVO, which means anti-aircraft defence. When I was telling you a moment ago that the zone of responsibility of the 1st PKB was there, I meant people -- men were taken from there and sent as infantry to Dobrinja 1 and 4. And the church at Veljine is just behind Dobrinja 4. Now, looking at this I can only speculate whether infantrymen were sent there to assist the armoured battalion as reinforcement. I don't know --

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. Witness --

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: -- it was just not --

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: -- let me stop you there. I'm not asking you to speculate. Now, the question was simply: This provision right here provides that there is -- that there is a battery from the 1st Sarajevo Brigade with one platoon on Veljine; correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: It's not a battalion, no question. It says very explicitly 1 weak anti-aircraft defence, self-propelled light artillery battery from the 1st Sarajevo Brigade, that means that they had very few men, and another platoon in the village of Vranjes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. Trapara, my question to you is simply this: That battery, not battalion, that battery was clearly on Veljine? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, can I please have 65 ter 30643. And, Your Honours, while we're waiting for that to come up this is a detail from map P3, e-court page 54. Now, if we could zoom in a little bit to the lower half of this map. That would do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. Trapara, you see from right around the middle, right to the left going in a south-westerly direction you see Miljevici; correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, you know this area well. Do you see where Vranjes is?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Between that and Dobrinja, that's where Veljine is; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, if we zoom in a little bit more on the lower half of this, you see almost --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Shin.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you -- apparently the witness has found Vranjes, I not -- yes, I see it. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: No, I'm sorry, Mr. President, I should have indicated to Your Honours as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, we have Miljevici and Vranjes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Please do, because I still don't see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Your Honours, if we look at the three flags we see in Cyrillic -- well, a CPK in the middle and immediately to the right something that looks like 4A -- AU -- yes, thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Trapara, I'd like you to focus on a flag depicted on this map. The bottom of this flag is just at the G of G. Kotorac, Gornji Kotorac. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, on that flag we see in Cyrillic letters OKB; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And that's the acronym for the armoured battalion you were speaking of; correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And finally on this map, as we see just below where it says G. Kotorac, this red line that we see, this thin red line made of dashes and dots, would it be correct that that's the border-line between the Sarajevo Mechanised Brigade and the next brigade over?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes. The neighbour is the Light Sarajevo Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Could I please tender this map, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 30643 receives number P6516, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Trapara, would it be correct that either this armoured battalion or the other armoured battalion also had T-55 tanks?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: How many tanks did they have?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: I cannot tell you exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like to move to a slightly different area now. In your statement or earlier today you were explaining about the three 82-millimetre mortars and we saw the location of that on the map earlier. Now, you've explained in previous testimony that you as company commander could ask for support from these mortars which were under the control of the battalion; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And this was in the Dragomir Milosevic testimony. You further explained specifically that you "personally as a commander could call on these mortars." And my question to you is: How was that done? Was that done by radio or was that done by something else?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: We did it in two ways, by radio and by telephone, wire telephone. We had a wire connection from the battalion command to my company. Thus, when I felt the need for mortars, I would call the superior command to get them to approve mortar action only in situations when we were directly attacked and my own life and the lives of my soldiers were in danger.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, who did you call specifically at the battalion command when you wanted the support of these mortars?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Somebody from the command. The duty officer if I was unable to get the commander of the battalion or his deputy, I would call the duty officer at the command of the battalion. The commander could not always be present; he was often in the field.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, you explained the circumstances under which you would make this call for mortar support. Let me ask you, would you, for example, call in mortar fire in response to sniper fire you were receiving from the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: I never called in mortar support in reaction to sniper fire because it would have been too risky for us. When there was sniper fire we mostly --

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, if the translation could continue. I wasn't sure if you were finished.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: I was about to say this: We neutralised sniper fire from our positions using the Browning 12.7-millimetres because we targeted directly those places from which we noticed the sniper firing at our positions and behind our lines at the population.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned a Browning. Is it -- would it be appropriate also in response to sniper fire to use rockets?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: I didn't have that capability. I didn't have rockets.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: I'm asking you whether as an infantry commander you think that would be an appropriate response to sniper fire?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, it's a hypothetical question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Asked and answered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, whether that's true or not, but at least it's a hypothetical question. Mr. Shin, if you could make it a factual question, then. But whether it would be appropriate to do something where the witness told us that he didn't have that facility available to him that --

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Okay. I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]...

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: -- Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. Trapara, you in your statement talk about receiving daily sniper fire and you've just described that a little bit now. Apart from the Browning was there anything else that you had available in your company to respond to sniper fire?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: We had an anti-aircraft gun, 20-millimetres, it was issued to us, to my company from supplies, PAT 20-millimetres, that means anti-aircraft machine-gun. In 1994 when the order came to remove heavy weapons at a certain distance from Sarajevo, we had to give it up.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. Trapara, would it also be correct that you could use rifles to neutralise a sniper?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Well, you can do it even with a pistol if you are that good a marksman. We could have, but a sniper fires two bullets and then runs away to a different area, to a different sector. And that happened every day. In my statement I said that throughout the war we were below Muslim forces --

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. Trapara --

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: -- Bogusevac and --

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: -- I'm sorry to stop you there but I think we're getting a little far afield from the line of topics we were discussing. Now, you were saying that -- what you were saying is of course that if you were a good marksman you could neutralise a sniper; that's what you said. Correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes. But you know what that means? That means finding a good sniper that would take out the sniper on the other side with a rifle, and that happened too.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, you described the possibility of calling your battalion command for 82-millimetre mortar support. Isn't it also the case that if your men's safety -- if their lives were in danger, you could call on the battalion command for any other assets that they had available to support your troops?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Shin, could I seek clarification of one of the previous answers?

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said, Witness, you said responding to sniper fire, you said: "That means finding a good sniper that would take out the sniper on the other side with a rifle and that happened too." Do I understand that in response to sniper fire you found good snipers that would take out the sniper on the other side, that that happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That would be in one case in a thousand, but it happened. We had few such men.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One in a thousand? That seems -- sounds very exceptional. Was that exceptional?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was really that exceptional that a sniper could take out a sniper. He really had to be master of his trade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, to be successful. But how often was it tried to eliminate a sniper on the other side by using snipers on your side?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The worst thing for me was that we didn't have any snipers at all. We didn't need snipers because we were -- we were on lower ground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But you said it happened, which suggests that at least there were snipers, if not in your own unit then nearby, to do this exceptional job?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I heard of such things, nowhere near me, but yes such cases existed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So the one out of thousands you do not even have personal knowledge about this happening?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Shin.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Trapara, continuing on with this issue of snipers. First, do you accept that in the 1st Sarajevo Mechanised Brigade there were considerable quantities of sniper weapons, optical equipment, and silencers for sniper rifles?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: At brigade level, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: In that light can we briefly have P675 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: This is an order from the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps command to all units. You can see at the bottom the signature of the commander, General Galic. Now let's go to point 1. It states: "Each brigade should set up a platoon-strength snipers group (30 + 1 soldiers). These should be supplied with sniper rifles, optical, and infrared, passive sights, silencers." Do you see that, Mr. Trapara?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, this would appear to refer to what were saying about battalion assets, battalions having snipers; correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: I've said the brigade had these assets. I just said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, that's right, you said brigades. I would like to go to point 2. It states: "These forces should immediately start training and carrying out assignments ..." And point 3 states: "Report to Corps Command by 2400 ..." Now, this order to all units in the SRK, do you accept that that means it would have gone to, as you say, the brigade level?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: By the way, you see that this document is number 20/15-1244, 1244. Let's move to another document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before you do, can I ask this question?

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Trapara, this order in the first paragraph says: "Each brigade should set up a platoon-strength snipers group ..." How do I understand that? Does it mean the brigade forms a platoon, which is armed with snipers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's what the document says, it's written there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Does that mean then that the sniper groups did not just end at the brigade, they went down to the platoon?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, by logic that should be so --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Not by logic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- but it didn't reach me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Not by logic, by this order.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, yes, according to the order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: If I could have P762 on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, while we're waiting for this document -- just one moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I misspoke, Ms. Stewart has corrected me, it's P672.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. Trapara, this is a document you've seen before. It's a report from the 1st Sarajevo Mechanised Brigade to the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps command. Now, you see at the bottom it's from Colonel Veljko Stojanovic, commander of the 1st Sarajevo Mechanised Brigade. We can see it begins: "Pursuant to your order, strictly confidential, number 20/15-1244 ..." And this is a report in response to the order from General Galic, the very document we just saw. And this, by the way, reflects the chain of command, right? The corps command issues an order to the brigades and the brigades report on the implementation of the order? You nodded your head; is that a "yes"? You nodded your head again. Please just say yes for the record.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Trapara, if you are nodding, that does not appear on the transcript so everyone will have to guess what your answer was. When you were nodding, you were confirming the accuracy of what Mr. Shin said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, a moment ago I did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: So on the chain of command -- in fact, we see at the stamp at the bottom of this document that the report was received at 2350 hours, obediently complying with the orders specification that reports were due to the corps command by 2400 hours. You see that; correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, you see that this document refers to various items that the 1st Sarajevo Mechanised Brigade possessed. I'm not going to read them all out, but you see, for example, the references to number 4, 7.9-millimetre sniper rifle, 12 pieces, and we see number 8, sniper rifle silencers, four pieces, and so on. All together there are 30 rifles listed among this equipment. So now do you accept that your brigade, this 1st Sarajevo Mechanised Brigade had these weapons, as indicated by the brigade commander?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: I said to you a moment ago that the brigade had that and there is nothing controversial here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Well then we'll continue. Right after this inventory at the bottom of this document we read: "As we don't have a special sniper unit, we have issued the sniper rifles to combatants in the subordinated units. "They are active when the combatants are in position ..." Now, first, subordinate units, that would mean the battalions; correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And you accept that the brigade commander issued these sniper rifles to combatants in the subordinated units and that they were indeed active as the commander has indicated here?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And we see further below that there is a request for further rifles and more silencers; correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, you've told this Court that the commander of the battalion was Aleksandar Petrovic, deputy was Milan Hrvacevic, and the assistant commander for intel and security was Dragan Maletic, all in the 2nd Battalion; correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: If I could have another document, please, this is 65 ter 30656. And let's just have the first page in both, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Trapara, do you see under number 19 Aleksandar Petrovic?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And there is also Milan Hrvacevic in number 8 and Dragan Maletic in number 14?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: At the top of this page we see the word "command," "komanda."

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: This would appear to be a list of personnel at the command of your battalion; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, can we please have page 3 in B/C/S and English page 3. I'll be flipping over to page 4 as well for the English.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: At the bottom half of this page, Mr. Trapara, do you see the word "snipers"? And on the B/C/S you can see that there are 11 names.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, this indicates that there were 11 snipers under the command of the battalion, not the brigade; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Your Honours, could I have this document given an MFI number? It will be used again with another witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, the number would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 30656 receives number P6517, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I may continue just for a few more minutes to finish this section?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Do you think that five minutes would do?

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please do so and we'll take a break after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Trapara, I'm going to remind you that you said in your statement that the Muslim units facing you had a large number of snipers. That was their major strength. I'm looking at paragraph 20. And there was almost daily sniping against Serbian positions and civilians. Now, as you say you had - and this is the same paragraph - "... no trained professional snipers ..." You've described the situation of the snipers, described the fact that you called the battalion for 82-millimetre mortar support. Did you ever ask the battalion command for sniper support?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Did you ever ask the battalion command about sniper assets?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: This is the first time I see this document. Now, whether this was hidden from me, I don't know. I don't know about this. I just know --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters did not hear the second part of the sentence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the first time I see this document and the signatures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could I invite you to repeat what you said after you said: What I do know ... and then what you then said was lost. You said: "I don't know about this. I just know ..."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What, what did you just know? Could you please repeat it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
