utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just know that none of the mentioned soldiers who are mentioned as snipers, none of these soldiers were from my unit. They didn't even come close to my unit. This is the first time I see this document today with these signatures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you tell us where you say they did not even come close to your unit, where they then were to be found, if not close to your unit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Believe me, I don't know the location.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So it could even be close to your unit if you don't know the location?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is possible for me only to make an assumption.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: I have a couple more questions but maybe after the break since I can't control how long those questions may take.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, then we'll take the break first. Mr. Shin, I think you have approximately 15 minutes left from your estimate of two hours. Is that -- I think we resumed at ten minutes to 11.00. We are now close to 12.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: I'll assume that you are right, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Shin, but your last question, was it answered, irrespective of whether the witness has seen this document for the first time, your question was: Did you ever ask the battalion for sniper assets?

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes, I was going to return to that question but I can have the answer now if the witness is available.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've said no. I did not ask the battalion for snipers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Not snipers but sniper assets. There were two separate questions. You were asked about snipers and sniper assets, in other words, guns themselves.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Neither. I asked for neither.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted out of the courtroom. We take a break of 20 minutes, Mr. Trapara. [The witness stands down].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We resume at 20 minutes past midday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: While we're waiting for the witness to be brought into the courtroom, Mr. Lukic, for the next witness - and there are no protective measures as far as I remember - Mr. Skrba, the -- I think on the basis of the first witness list we concluded that the lower estimate would be the valid one, while we had then 1 hour and 30 minutes and 45 minutes, so we expected 45 minutes to be the time you would need but now --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It is 45 minutes. I just checked --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's 45 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- with Mr. Stojanovic since it's his witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. And not 1 hour and 30 minutes. That's been clarified. We can proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Shin, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. Trapara, I'd like to move to a different topic right now. I'd like to discuss an incident on October 15th, 1991, involving charges of the illegal possession of weapons and explosives and involving you. Could you please tell this Court what this case involved so they have a full picture and a full understanding of what this was about.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: In my statement, at the very outset of the statement, I said that in the month of September 1991 I saw Jusuf Prazina, nicknamed Juka, with his paramilitary units, and I saw them a lot every day. They instilled fear amongst the population of Lukavica with their sporadic gun-fire --

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. Trapara, if I could interrupt you there. My apologies. Perhaps I should have been more specific. Could you please describe your arrest for this incident and what happened afterwards.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: On the 15th of October, 1991, around 11.00 in the evening my uncle asked me whether I could go with him to Miljevici on a truck so that we could get a load. At first I didn't know what this was all about. When we arrived there, the village of Miljevic, that is, next to a warehouse and a chicken farm at the time some people said "Ignjatije, load this on to that truck and get going." Also, some young men loaded this - I really don't know why I went in the first place - these young men put these boxes on the truck within 10 or 15 minutes --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could all other microphones please be switched off. We cannot hear the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- we went in the direction of Lukavica. Can we hear each other now? Towards the area of Prljavo Brdo. As soon as we stopped this truck, within ten minutes or so a patrol car of the police arrived and three policemen got out. I personally knew two of them. One of them was called Jure, he was the commander, and the other one was Sulejman, Zoll [phoen], and the third one arrived later -- actually later I heard that his name was Pajdakovic [phoen], Sajuci [phoen]. They just asked then who the driver of that truck was. My uncle Ignjatije said: I. One of the policemen got on to the truck with him and the other two got into their own car and then they went in the direction of Vrace. I went back to my own home, and then the next day, the following day, that is, I went to work as usual. I worked at Post Office II in Sarajevo at the new railway station. I worked there for 10 or 12 days until two military policemen came and then they took me in. They took me to the Viktor Bubanj prison. I was detained there for 28 days. After that, I went back to my job, that is to say in November, and I worked all the way up until the 3rd of April. I remember that very well. It was the holiday of Bajram. From that day onwards, for personal and security reasons, I did not go to work. It was impossible to get through. There were barricades there, et cetera. That is what I have to say about that incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Can I seek clarification on one issue. You said your uncle was asked who was the driver, "he said: I." Did you mean to say that he himself was the driver or that you were the driver?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. My uncle was the driver of this Zastava.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And could you tell us what was loaded, finally, whether you have any knowledge, because that's the missing part of the story? What was found in that car? What was in those boxes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't know. Believe me. These were boxes and I could just assume --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No, please. Do you know now what was found in those boxes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now I do know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Tell us, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I read a report of the MUP of the SRBiH, that is to say the Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I think it was dated the 16th of October and it is stated there unequivocally --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please tell us, apart from what you read in a report, what was found in those boxes according to this report.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What was found was semiautomatic rifles. Also, this other thing, it was called "dobosari," they used ammunition for pistols, and also there was a certain amount of ammunition there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How many semiautomatic rifles were in there as reported?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know exactly. Believe me, I don't know the exact number. To this day I do not know the exact number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Shin.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. Trapara, you've referred to a police bulletin or a police report.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Could I have 65 ter 30639 on the screen. And if we go to the first page. While it's coming up, I'll describe what it is. It's a bulletin of significant daily events dated 16th of October, 1991, and at the top of the cover page it reads: "Socialist Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Ministry of the Interior." Now let's go to page 2 in English and 2 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, I'll orient you to where I'm going, Mr. Trapara. Do you see the reference in the top third of the page with a line beginning with the words "Naime, radnici ..." Now, first of all, this is the report that you were just talking about, the police report; that's correct, right?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, we see that it states that: "At about 0200 hours on the 15th of October, in the village of Ivanici, policemen at the Novo Sarajevo public security station stopped a freight vehicle that was being driven by its owner, Ignjatije Trapara. The truck was stopped at a second attempt after it failed to stop when the patrol first flagged it down." That's what the report reads, correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Okay. Now I'll move a few lines down where the cargo is addressed. Now, the Judges have asked you what this was cargo was. You've given an answer. You've seen this report before. Now let's see what it says. "The following items were found in the truck: Two hand-held launchers, two optical sights with the original boxes, two hand-held launcher mounts, two cleaning brushes for hand-held launchers, four wooden boxes containing 40 semi-automatic rifles with corresponding technical sheets, ammunition pouchs, and cleaning kits, seven semi-automatic rifles, four wooden boxes containing 3.600, 7.9-millimetre rounds, eight wooden boxes with 8.960, 7.62-millimetre rounds, and one box containing two M-53 light machine-guns with supplementary equipment, technical sheets, and cleaning kits ..." Did I read that right?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that this is considerably more than what you just told the Judges when they had asked you more than once what was in the cargo?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Well, I didn't know, I didn't know what the content was of this cargo.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Well, you say now that you didn't know, but let's go back to see what you said in the Dragomir Milosevic case.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: If I could have a moment, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps meanwhile I ask one question. The report states that you tried to flee. What was the reason for that? Did it happen and what was the reason if it happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Believe me, it did not happen. I said a moment ago I was of no interest to them at all. They just asked who the driver of the truck was. The following day I went to work as usual, as I said a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So you said when they report that you tried to escape that's just not true? Because that was my question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's not true. That's not true.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You did not run away?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Shin.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: But, Mr. Trapara, you accept that that's what the police report reads of course?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Well, police reports are not always truthful.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Shin.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If a report is so clear in its reading, then whether the witness confirms that it says so only if there's any matter which could reasonably be in dispute, but otherwise the Chamber reads that that's what the report tells us.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes, there's one other sentence which is relevant that I will point you to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, please do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: If we could on this document go to the English page 3 and the B/C/S page 3 as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Trapara, in the B/C/S this is in the upper third. This is a sentence that was not previously read to you in your prior testimonies. It -- and I'll read it out to you. I'll read it out to you now. It states: "The search for Predrag Trapara, 28, and Slobodan Trapara, 39, postmen at the Sarajevo Post Office II is continuing." That certainly suggests that they were looking for you, doesn't it?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Is it possible for me to work, to go to work the very next day all the way up until April 1992, and there I was working and then somebody writes this up and says that I was trying to escape? I cannot understand that. That report, that list that I got concerning employment after Dayton, and everything is stated there, that I worked, that I was at my job until the 4th of April, I cannot believe that they say that I tried to escape.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. Trapara, I'll return to this issue, but right now I want to return first to what we were discussing earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And if I could briefly go into private session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We move into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And while waiting for that I would just note that I'm moving into private session because it requires a portion of the Milosevic -- I won't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you wait for the confirmation that we are in private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Shin, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. Trapara, now even after you had read this police report in response to questions from the Court, you didn't give the full explanation of what it was, did you? You left out -- as we saw, you left out two machine-guns; that's correct, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes, I left it out but it's written in the report.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes. And you left out some other things as well, but I'm going to move to a few other issues here. Now, today you told the Judges that you went back to work in your post office for 10 to 12 day. Do you recall that in earlier testimony, perhaps to you a small difference, in an earlier testimony you said that you went back to work for seven days before the military police came to get you. That's correct, is it?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Well, all right. I mean, a man cannot remember everything that happened 20 years ago in a five-day period, five days here or there. I cannot remember precisely. But if we're talking about a certain period, it could be seven days later or seven days earlier.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Trapara, you've been asked about the contents of this truck. This is the third case you've been asked about the contents of this truck. Now, in the first -- in the Dragomir Milosevic case, do you recall that it took Defence counsel three questions for you to even begin discussing the contents of that truck; do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: In which case?

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: In the Dragomir Milosevic case.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And even after that, in the Karadzic case when you were asked about this and you were asked what the cargo was, your initial response was that it merely held these "dobosari" pistols and some semi-automatics; correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Isn't it clear that you are trying to minimise the nature of this incident, the gravity of this incident, and your involvement, at least you're trying to minimise it until you're confronted with the police report?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: I wasn't trying to minimise it. I wasn't sure how much of everything there was until I read this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: I'm going to move on now to ask you about what happened after -- what happened after this incident. Can you tell us in terms of criminal procedure you say that -- I can't recall if you explained. Did you end up going to court and what happened afterwards?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: I ended up before a military court and we were sentenced by the former JNA. Our trial was held at Viktor Bubanj.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And it's correct that at that time of course, as you say, that was the JNA that held the barracks? I'll move on since you've already answered that question. Did you receive a fine as well?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: We did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: With that, Your Honours, I would tender 65 ter 30639.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 30639 receives number P6518, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Trapara, I'd like to move on back to this issue of humanitarian convoys. In your statement --

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, that's paragraphs 21 and 22.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: -- in your statement you address humanitarian assistance for the Muslim-held part of town and you explain that you always let that through. In the Karadzic testimony you were shown this document which is now D462, if we could just have that up briefly. At that time in the Karadzic testimony you were asked -- when you were asked about this document, you answered: "When it comes to this order, I have to say that I could have learned about it through the battalion command. That was the only way for me to be aware of this order, but I never received this order from the battalion commander nor was I aware of it." So you weren't of course aware of that document? I'm not sure what the translation was, Mr. Trapara, I'm not trying to ask a complicated question. I'm just simply asking you to confirm that, as you said in your Karadzic testimony, you were not aware of that document?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, we don't need to bring up this other document, but regarding document D461 you were asked about that as well in the Karadzic testimony and your answer at that time was: "At that time I was a young man. I was a company commander. I was a local guy. People knew me and I did not have access to information at such a high level. This was a very high level for me." So once again, that's a document you really didn't know anything about; correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, you addressed also a document earlier today that was P2050, and regarding that document as well - and this was about humanitarian assistance also - you were asked about that in Karadzic again. You answered: "I didn't know anything about that at that time. I knew Mr. Abdic well but only from the media like everyone else. I didn't know that things had to be done the way as is described here." So you didn't know about that document either; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: It's not quite clear to me what documents you're talking about. I don't have anything in front of me here.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: That's fair enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Can we have P2050 on the screen.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And earlier when you were talking I didn't have anything in front of me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: This is the most recent document we were talking about, P2050, and in the Karadzic case you had been read part of paragraph 6.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you perhaps briefly introduce the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes, of course, Mr. President. This is a code cable from Mr. Akashi to Mr. Annan. It's dated 14 March 1995. And if we go to paragraph 6 I'll read the relevant passage. The first sentence reads: "On the subject of freedom of movement, particularly with regard to the delivery of humanitarian assistance, General Mladic was very obstructive. He insisted on absolute parity between what is delivered to the Bosnian Serbs and what is delivered to the enclaves ..."

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Trapara, you were asked in the Karadzic case by the Prosecution whether on the basis of this you would accept that there was indeed a policy at the highest levels of the Bosnian Serb army in the highest levels of the Bosnian Serb political organs to deliberately obstruct the delivery of humanitarian assistance. And at that question your response was what I mentioned earlier, that you didn't know anything about that at the time. Correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to move on to paragraph 14 of your statement. You don't need to refer to that. I'll tell you what it says. You say civilians in your area on Serbian territory were "frightened by frequent shelling from the Muslim side ..." Now, it would be logical, wouldn't it, that heavy shelling would frighten them more than light shelling? Mr. Trapara, we're not on that document now. Perhaps if we could remove the document from the screens and I can return to the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Shin, and the Chamber would prefer if you would not ask the witness what is logical or not but rather to ask what he knows.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes, of course, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Logic is not the easiest thing in a courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. Trapara, my question to you: You said in your statement that civilians, Serb civilians, on your side in Serbian territory were frightened by the frequency of shelling from the Muslim side. They were more frightened by heavier shelling than they were by very light shelling; correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, you would agree that civilians on the other side, Muslim civilians, would likewise be frightened by shelling?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And you agree that they would also be frightened more by heavy shelling than by light shelling?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: So you would agree -- well, let me put it this way. Would you agree that shelling was heavier from the Serb side than it was from the ABiH side?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: At the beginning, at the line where I was, yes; but then from the middle until the end it was more or less even. So at the beginning of the war what you said is correct, but from the middle until the end of the war what I said stands. They armed themselves more and more each day, so we were equally matched.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: My question to you wasn't about whether you were both equally matched. My question to you whether you would agree that the shelling was heavier from the Serb side than from the ABiH side?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It is asked and answered.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It is, Mr. Shin. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: I'd like to now turn to the discussion that we had earlier about the 20-millimetre anti-aircraft gun that you had, the PAT. Now, how long was it that you had these guns -- I'm sorry, that gun.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: From November 1992 until the order in 1994 I think when the order came for the heavy artillery to be relocated from Sarajevo to I don't know how many kilometres back, until that time. So according to that order it was specified what sort of weaponry could remain. The 20-millimetre PAT anti-aircraft gun had to be moved.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And when in 1994 was it that it had to be moved?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: I can't remember the exact month.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Do you recall in prior testimony that you said that that occurred in August of 1994?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: It was more or less when General Milosevic assumed the post of corps commander, around that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And to the best of your recollection, would that have been around August or some other time?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: I really couldn't confirm that now.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Was it later in 1994 or was it earlier?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I have to object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness apparently remembers that it was around the moment that General Milosevic assumed the post of corps commander. Could the parties not agree on when that was?

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That seems not to be a matter which creates great dispute. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes, and I don't need to do this with the witness. So I'll just simply ask:

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. Trapara, are you aware that the agreement on the withdrawal of heavy weapons was made in February of 1994?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: I don't remember the exact date. I know that it was in 1994, in the first half of 1994. I can't remember the exact date. It's been a long time since then.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Well, we can check later to see when it was that General Milosevic took his post since you've specified that at least. I'd like to move to another area and this relates to your statement where you talk about several locations and geographical features.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And for Your Honours, that's paragraph 6.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: You mentioned Stupsko Brdo. That's not in your zone of responsibility, is it?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: You mention Zuc, that's not in your area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Nor are these other places that you've listed there as being under BH army control, and these include Hum, Cordon, Colina Kapa, Bistrik, Kula, Sokolje, none of those are in your area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: They didn't have to be in my area of responsibility, but everybody knew that the B&H army was at those locations.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now in your Dragomir Milosevic testimony you were asked this question: "Some of the inner hills, the ones closer to the city, were held by the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, but as you go back further away from the town you get to hills that were held by the Army of Republika Srpska; isn't that correct?" And your answer was: "To the depths of the territory, yes." You stand by that; correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Now, there was also some discussion in that case about the positioning of various elevations, particularly with regards to Debelo Brdo and an elevation known as Grad. Now, I'm not going to get into that with you now but I'll just put this question to you: There are indirect and direct means of fire; correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And indirect means of fire, as the phrase would indicate, does not require a direct line of sight?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: And now finally my last question to you, Mr. Trapara: Are you aware of any military prosecutions, administrative discipline, inquiries, investigations, or similar into allegations that soldiers of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps committed war crimes during the period when you were a member of the 2nd Battalion?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Specifically for my unit, no, but as for that section of the corps that you are talking about, war crimes were committed by people who were not members of any military formation. They were -- I don't even know what I could call them. They were so-called free shooters. They did not belong to any military command and they didn't have any military honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Mr. Trapara, my question was specifically about the soldiers of the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps, not about people who were not part of the army.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: I don't think any war crimes happened in our sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Shin. One additional question, Mr. Trapara. You told us that crimes were committed by those who were not members of the army. Could you tell us something about that? What crimes do you remember were committed and by whom were they committed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I would not like to mention specific names now because all these young men have been tried and convicted by the BH court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then nevertheless I would like you to tell us the names of those that come to your mind at this moment.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. I feel very awkward should I mention the names now, but we all know their names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well this Court does not; that's the reason why I'm asking. If you would prefer to go into private session, that's okay as far as I'm concerned. But would you like to answer the question in private session and then we move into private session?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you insist, I can give you one name. I can't remember any more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You know of one name only, one person only, of what you called free shooters?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay. Who was it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Are we in private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No. If you want us to turn into private session, we move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Mr. Shin.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I wanted to catch us before we left private session. There is a correction in a name and perhaps we can do that now or towards the end, whenever is more convenient.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's do it at the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: We would still need the witness for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, that's fine. Mr. Lukic, how much time would you need for re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: In between 10 to 15 minutes, maybe 10.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you could -- if you would do it in 10 and then we would hear from Mr. Shin, because then we are just a little bit over the one hour. But if you would re-examine the witness now. You'll be re-examined, Mr. Trapara, by Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I would like to have P672 in the e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do you remember, Mr. Trapara, that you were asked about this document?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Do you have any direct knowledge that this document was really acted upon? In other words, were snipers really distributed in reality and do you know to whom?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: I did not know and I still don't know today to whom exactly the snipers were distributed, I mean I didn't know until the moment when I saw it in another document a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Considering the position of your unit, could you describe it more precisely? What were you able to see of the positions on enemy territory?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: From our positions, we were able to see only two rows of houses from the Mojmilo hill, down the slope towards us. And the BH Army had positions inside those houses, they had trenches outside, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Could you explain why that is so?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: On that map the Prosecutor showed a moment ago there were three main features, Bogusevac 860 metres altitude and the two other features, all these three dominant features were held by the Muslim side.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: The depth of the territory held by the Muslim side was behind the hills; correct?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Now I would like to see P2050 again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: When waiting for it to come up, Mr. Lukic, I was a bit confused by your question about whether it really happened, what we saw in that document, because the document apparently describes what was done, not what was intended to be done but what was done. So therefore I was a bit confused by your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I was just checking with the witness if he has any knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In today's transcript, you don't have to bother about it, I'll read it out to you, on page 64, lines 7 through 13, my colleague Mr. Shin from the Prosecution put to you that in a previous trial the suggestion was made to you that the highest levels obstructed the passage of convoys, and in response you confirmed that's what's written in the document. I want to ask you once again: Did it ever happen on the ground controlled by your unit that a convoy was not allowed through?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: No, it didn't happen. Maybe also because this order was in place although I didn't know about it. Maybe I even violated some orders that I was not aware of, but I let every convoy pass without exception.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: There was one convoy in which the military police found seven rifles.

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: That's correct. That was at the intersection in Lukavica by the local commune building.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Was that convoy allowed through after the rifles were removed?

utterances.speaker: PREDRAG TRAPARA
utterances.text: I don't know how the corps military police got intelligence about these rifles. I was at an observation point just watching this incident, and the convoy carrying flour continued to Grbavica. So the rifles were removed and the convoy went on its way after detailed inspection, that's true.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Trapara.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. We have nothing further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Lukic. If there was -- do you have --

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: No, nothing further from me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- any other questions apart from the one you had.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yeah, just the one correction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Can we -- we have to deal with it in private session?

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Yes, because it arises from a portion of the private session testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we will briefly move for what will be the last question, Mr. Trapara, into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Mr. Trapara, this concludes your testimony in this court. I would like to thank you very much for coming a long way to The Hague and for having answered all the questions that were put to you by the parties and by the Bench, and I wish you a safe return home again. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll take a break and we'll resume at quarter to 2.00 and then we have another half-hour to start the testimony of the next witness, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Is the Defence ready to call its next witness? Mr. Ivetic, I -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could the witness be escorted into the courtroom. Mr. Ivetic, I see that you're present. There is an issue the Chamber would like to discuss with the parties, but we prefer not to have the witness wait now for half an hour then to find out that we have not started his examination, but tomorrow we'll certainly find time to deal with the matter. I don't know to what extent it has already been discussed with the Prosecution what this topic is we would like to discuss in private session; if not, you'll be informed about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Skrba, I presume. Before you give evidence, the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration. May I invite you to do so. The text is handed out to you by the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Skrba. Please be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You'll first be examined by Mr. Stojanovic. You'll find him to your left. Mr. Stojanovic is counsel for Mr. Mladic. Mr. Stojanovic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Mr. Skrba.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: For the record, could you please state your name and surname slowly.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA
utterances.text: My name is Dusan Skrba.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please tell the Court whether you gave Mr. Mladic's Defence team a statement pertaining to the questions that we had put to you?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, could we please have the following document in e-court: 65 ter 1D01610. Also I would like us to focus on the first page of that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Skrba, are these your personal details and is this your signature?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'd like us to have a look at the last page of this document. It has a total of six pages and in the lower right-hand corner there is a signature. Is that your signature, Mr. Skrba?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now I'm going to put the following to you. Today if I were to put the same questions to you like those contained in this statement, would you give the same answers now also after having made the solemn declaration?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA
utterances.text: Yes, 99 per cent to the best of my knowledge and recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Would your answers contain the truth concerning these events?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA
utterances.text: It would always be the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth as best I can relate it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to tender Mr. Dusan Skrba's statement into evidence, 1D01610, that is its 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: No objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Skrba, may I take it that you recently had an opportunity to review what is written down as your statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D1610 receives number D463, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D463 is admitted into evidence. You may proceed, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, also I would like to suggest that along with the witness's statement another document be admitted, 1D02039, that's its 65 ter number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's one out of the two associated exhibits announced. Any objection against this associated exhibit?

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: If that's the one -- I believe that's the one ending with the 39 number, no objections. Just a question about the practicality of being able to see what's depicted there. I'm not sure if there's a way of making that more visible, since it's a rather large map, as it comes up on e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, any practical solution for that? Is it --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm afraid we cannot do more than this. We did our best. In P3 this document is contained as taken from the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps and as transmitted to this collection by the OTP. So objectively speaking we were not in a position to improve this in any way. If the OTP has some technical capacity to improve this further, we would gratefully accept that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Which page in the court binder of P3?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At this moment, I haven't got P3 with me, but already by tomorrow I could provide you with the relevant page number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, and otherwise we have to rely on the old magnifying glass which will assist us in this era of -- Madam Registrar, the number would be?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D2039 receives number D464, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And is admitted into evidence. I wanted to refer to the era of the electronics. Please proceed, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] By your leave, Your Honour, I would like to read the summary of Dusan Skrba's statement that has been admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I take it that it's even shorter than the summary of the previous witness. I would say 65 ter summaries sometimes assist. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Dusan Skrba, a witness, was born in 1949 in the municipality of Ilidza near Sarajevo. Before the war broke out he lived and worked in Sarajevo. During his military service, he graduated from the reserve officers' school, artillery. From the 5th of March, 1992, when he was mobilised as a reserve officer of the JNA, he remained involved in the military practically up until the end of the war. When the 1st Romanija Brigade was established, he was appointed commander of the mixed artillery battalion. His unit was deployed practically on the southern outskirts of Sarajevo and it supported the infantry units at the front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. SHIN
utterances.text: Sorry, the witness appears to be having difficulties with something in his system, the computer system I mean.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do not know -- are there any difficulties you are experiencing in this --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I just wanted to say when -- that this happened when the 1st Sarajevo Brigade was formed and that's where I served and that's where I defended my people. That was the first one that came into existence when the JNA left. It wasn't the Romanija Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Skrba, apparently it has not been explained to you properly what the purpose of this exercise is. Since you are not telling us everything viva voce, we know what is in your statement. Now, the public who is following these proceedings are not aware of what is in your statement, so therefore it's just a summary, it's just a short outline of what is to be found in your statement. It's not evidence. You don't have to comment on it. We will focus on your statement. Mr. Stojanovic, again you come with all kind of details which are totally irrelevant for the purpose. The purpose exclusively is to inform the public about what is approximately in the statement and where the witness was born and at what time, et cetera, that's all totally irrelevant. So therefore why not next time use your 65 ter summary and leave it as short as that. If you would agree with that, I would read the 65 ter summary, unless you have it, so that we do not lose ourselves in details irrelevant for the purpose.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Your Honour. I'm going to shorten this and it's going to be very succinct, succinctly what the witness said. The witness testified saying that he received orders only from the command of the 1st Sarajevo Brigade and it never happened that anyone went beyond the chain of command and control and he never received direct orders from General Mladic. The witness said that throughout the war there was a team of UNPROFOR monitors along the positions of his unit throughout the war. They slept there and they were aware of each and every move made by this artillery unit. The artillery piece operators could only approach artillery pieces on the basis of his order. If artillery fire were opened, then he'd have to inform the UN observers and show them the positions that were attacked by BiH army forces. After opening fire he was duty-bound to submit reports on the spot to members of the observer mission of the UN. This witness and all members of his unit never had any intention to cause civilian casualties or terrorise the civilians in any way. This witness confirms that throughout the war he never received any order, orally or in writing, to attack public transportation vehicles in the part of town that was under the control of the Muslim authorities. On the contrary, there was a standing order stating that fire should not be opened at civilian targets in the city. 99 per cent of all members of his unit were inhabitants of Sarajevo. These were -- they were literally the people's army, they were defending their homes. Also, the witness is aware of the fact that within the positions of his units within that area on the southern outskirts of Sarajevo on the 28th of August 1995 when the tragedy at Markale took place, and it is marked as G18 in the indictment, there were no mortars of 120-millimetres. The witness claims that mortars of 120-millimetre calibre and above were moved out of Sarajevo, out of a diameter of 20 kilometres. The witness very directly states that in the area of Miljevici also on the road near the village of Studankovici [phoen] towards the tower at Trebevic there was not a firing position for a 120-millimetre mortar. Your Honours, this would be a brief summary of the witness's statement and with your permission I would like to put a few questions to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may do so. For the coming witnesses, unless you have pointed at exceptional circumstances, the summary should be limited to not than 35 lines in the transcript. That is a little bit over one page of 25 lines. That's your guidance for the days to come. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Skrba, we who are not soldiers, especially not artillerymen, could you please give us an explanation as to what a mixed artillery battalion is?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA
utterances.text: A mixed artillery battalion consists of several different artillery pieces of different calibres, and let me say it is 120-millimetre mortars, howitzers, VBRs, and the rest that was available in my area of responsibility.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Tell the Court specifically, during the war which weapons and artillery pieces did your mixed artillery battalion have?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA
utterances.text: My unit had three batteries of howitzers, D-30, 120-millimetres, four pieces respectively; also a battery of VBRs, Plamen 1 with four pieces; and two mortar batteries of 120-millimetres, M-75, 12 pieces.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I would just like for you to repeat something for me. What is the area that your mixed artillery battalion defended throughout this front line area?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA
utterances.text: It was a very long front line. We had two rings because we had this double encirclement. The front part of the front line when we are facing the city, that was from Zlatiste, Kozlja Cupula [phoen], Kovaci, all the way down the Miljacka river, Dobrinja, Mojmilo, to the back side of the Zeljeznica river-bed. We called this area Stari Krtelj [phoen], and behind us there was Mount Igman, Trnovo, Jahorina, and the rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: My colleague has warned me that the last part of your answer was not in the transcript and that is the position that you mentioned behind you or in this outer ring, as you say?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA
utterances.text: In -- mostly so far the questions had to do with Sarajevo and civilian structures, and so we're talking Zlatiste, Kozlja Cupula, Kovac, along the Miljacka river via Mojmilo, Dobrinja, and then it ended with the Zeljeznica river-bed. That was the inner ring. All the questions so far referred to this inner area exclusively. As for the outer area where we had considerable casualties is something that nobody really put any questions to me about.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please give us those positions of the Bosnia and Herzegovina army that were behind your positions to the south from where you were exposed to artillery and other types of fire.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA
utterances.text: Until the action Lukavac 93, we had a lot of casualties from our back, where the positions of the B&H army were: Igman, Treskavica, Rogovi, Crna Rijeka, and others. And this is something that we were free of only after the Lukavac 93 action was executed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In order for this to be a bit more clear to us, can we look at document 1D02040 in e-court, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to ask for the usher's assistance here.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And also for you to assist us, please. Could the usher please help you mark the positions that I will ask you to mark. Mr. Skrba, please don't mark anything yet. We need to do that step by step together with the transcript. So could you please mark where the command of the 1st Artillery Division was. Perhaps if you need to zoom in on to the southern sector.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we zoom in on that section a little bit more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic, you are aware that once we have zoomed in, we can't zoom out any further. So if we zoom in --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's clear. I think that we can zoom in once and then -- yes, that's correct, Your Honour, that would be then the spot from which we will not be needing any more enlargement.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, can you find your way around on this map then?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Which part you would focus on? Because it's -- everything is now in the middle. If you would --

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to ask the witness to mark the place where the command of the mixed artillery division was. Could he please mark that with a circle.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: For the transcript, could you please tell the Trial Chamber the name of this area that you marked.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA
utterances.text: This place was called Ujzojnice [phoen].

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And are you able to tell the Trial Chamber which of the pieces that you mentioned that were part of the mixed artillery division were situated near the command post of the mixed artillery division?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA
utterances.text: All the pieces that I mentioned, all the batteries were in an area surrounding that spot some 300 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. We will now be dealing with the matter of 120-millimetre mortars. So I would like to ask you first to mark with a circle the places where --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you first invite the witness to put letters to this first circle so that we later do know what is which circle.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Of course I can do that. I actually meant to do that later.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, could you please indicate -- could you put the letters KMAD next to this circle.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, the witness now has written different letters there. Could the usher assist in removing the text and then could you please clearly instruct what letters to write but we'll first remove the ones we have now.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Skrba, once again could you please place the following letters next to the circle, K, komanda, MAD, mixed artillery division.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And thank you for your help.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you permit me, Your Honour, I would now like to ask the witness to mark the spots where he remembers the 120-millimetre mortar batteries were located.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA
utterances.text: Should I mark those spots?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And could you please place the letters MB-120 next to those two circles.

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And then I will finish my questioning today with just this question: How far were the 120-millimetre mortars from the command of the mixed artillery division where you were located?

utterances.speaker: DUSAN SKRBA
utterances.text: 250 metres as the crow flies.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would like to stop with my examination of the witness today and I would need 20 more minutes to finish my examination of this witness. And also could we save this image because we will be using the document again and I would like to also tender this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Madam Registrar -- now, all the markings seems to have been gone. They are saved. Under what number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Document 1D2040 as marked by the witness receives number D465, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And would you -- do you intend to ask the witness to make further markings on it? Then we'll just mark it for identification and we'll start tomorrow with it so that we have a full picture at the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then, Madam Registrar, it will be marked for identification under this number. Mr. Skrba, we'll adjourn for the day and I would like to instruct you that you should not speak or communicate in whatever way with whomever about your testimony, that is, your testimony given today or testimony still to be given tomorrow. Would you please keep that in mind. And then we would like to see you back tomorrow morning at 9.30. And I suggest to the parties that we will finish the examination-in-chief, then deal with the matter I indicated before, and that then most likely after the first break the witness will be cross-examined. You may follow the usher. We would like to see you back tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We adjourn for the day and we'll resume tomorrow, Wednesday, the 21st of May, at 9.30 in the morning in this same courtroom, I.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 21st day of May, 2014, at 9.30 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 2.16 p.m.,
